title: Reject text index with min_token_len greater than max_token_len
body:
## Summary

Fixes #10578 — a full-text index configured with `min_token_len > max_token_len` is accepted by both REST and gRPC, but the token filter then rejects every token, silently building an empty index.

This change rejects the inverted range at validation time, mirroring the existing integer-index `lookup`/`range` check.

## Changes

- **`lib/segment/src/data_types/index.rs`**: add `validate_text_index_params` and a `Validate` impl for `TextIndexParams`.
- **`lib/segment/src/types.rs`**: wire `TextIndexParams::validate` into `PayloadSchemaParams::validate` (REST path).
- **`lib/api/src/grpc/validate.rs`**: add a `Validate` impl for the gRPC `TextIndexParams` and call it from `IndexParams::validate`.
- **`lib/edge/ffi/src/payload_index.rs`**: enforce the same rule in the FFI conversion (returns `InvalidArgument`).
- **Tests**: unit test for `validate_text_index_params` and an OpenAPI regression test asserting a 422 with the new error message.

## Testing

- Unit test covers valid (`min < max`, `min == max`, unset) and invalid (`min > max`) cases.
- OpenAPI test asserts `PUT /collections/{name}/index` with `min_token_len: 10, max_token_len: 5` returns 422.

Note: I was unable to run `cargo test` locally (no Rust toolchain installed), so CI will need to confirm compilation and tests.

* [x] Have you added an explanation of what your changes do and why you'd like us to include them?
* [x] Have you written new tests for your core changes, as applicable?
* [x] Have you successfully ran tests with your changes locally?

## What this changes and why

`JapaneseTokenizer::tokenize` post-processed each token inline instead of routing it through `TokensProcessor::process_token_cow`. Four options that a text index accepts therefore never applied to text the tokenizer treated as Japanese: `min_token_len`, `max_token_len`, `stemmer` and `ascii_folding`.

It also checked stopwords against the raw surface and lowercased afterwards, the opposite of `process_token_cow`'s order. `StopwordsFilter` stores its entries lowercased when `lowercase` is on but does not lowercase the token it is asked about, so a capitalised stopword reached the index: with the default `lowercase: true` and a stopword set containing `"it"`, the token `It` survived while the identical word in a Latin-script document was dropped.

The sibling branch in `multilingual.rs` already sends every token through `process_token_cow`, `TokensProcessor`'s own doc comment says it "applies all configured options to the token", and `TextIndexParams` documents all five unconditionally, with `tokenizers/mod.rs` building the processor with no per-tokenizer branching. So this makes the two branches agree rather than adding behaviour. The surface is cloned up front because `iter_tokens()` borrows from the sentence, which the existing TODO above the loop already notes.

## Test plan

`dev` at `aefcb71b0ff46b37918c3ca36906ab7eb39c7ec8`, toolchain 1.98.0 (the repo's MSRV), aarch64-apple-darwin. The vaporetto model is `include_bytes!`-ed from the repo, so these run fully offline.

<details>
<summary>Command output</summary>

Before the fix, with only the new tests added:

```
test ...japanese::test::test_min_token_len_is_applied ... FAILED
test ...japanese::test::test_stopwords_are_matched_case_insensitively ... FAILED
test ...japanese::test::test_max_token_len_is_applied ... FAILED

min_token_len = 2 must drop shorter tokens, got ["日本", "語", "の", "テキスト", "です"]
max_token_len = 2 must drop longer tokens, got ["日本", "語", "の", "テキスト", "です"]
the lowercase stopword "it" must drop the capitalised token "It", got ["日本", "語", "の", "テキスト", "です", "it", "s", "used", ...]

test result: FAILED. 3 passed; 3 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1134 filtered out
```

With the fix, all tokenizer tests:

```
$ cargo test -p segment --lib tokenizers::
test result: ok. 30 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1110 filtered out; finished in 0.90s
```

And the wider text index suite, to check nothing else moved:

```
$ cargo test -p segment --lib full_text_index
test result: ok. 101 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 1039 filtered out; finished in 2.40s
```

</details>

The two pre-existing japanese tests use `TokensProcessor::default()`, which has no stopwords, no stemmer and no length bounds, so their exact token lists are unchanged. Gates: `cargo +nightly fmt --all -- --check` clean; `cargo clippy -p segment --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean, no warnings; `sg scan --config tools/ast-grep/sgconfig.yml` clean.

The assertions are properties over the emitted tokens rather than fixed token lists, so they do not pin vaporetto's segmentation, which #8595 shows is still in flux. The existing tests in this module do use exact lists; I did not change them.

## Migration note and checklist

Indexes built from text the tokenizer treated as Japanese will change, because tokens those options should have removed now are, and capitalised stopwords now drop. A collection indexed with any of `min_token_len`, `max_token_len`, `stemmer` or `ascii_folding` configured has to be re-created; one that configures none is unaffected.

<details>
<summary>AI disclosure</summary>

Per "Contributing with AI" in `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`:

- `[AI] fix(tokenizer): run the japanese branch through TokensProcessor` — the only commit here, generated with an AI coding assistant.

The initial intent I gave it: find a deterministic, offline-reproducible defect where the repository's own code or tests already state the expected behaviour and the code does something else, preferring one the repository documents; reproduce before opening a PR. Which options the vaporetto branch skipped, and the stopword ordering, came from reading `tokens_processor.rs`, `multilingual.rs` and `stop_words/mod.rs` and comparing their orderings, not from an assumed answer. Every command output above was run and read. I am responsible for this change and can explain any part of it.

</details>

title: fix: reject empty multi-dense RawVector instead of panicking
body:
## Why

Fixes #9954.

`TryFrom<grpc::RawVector> for VectorInternal` converted `MultiDense` with the infallible `From<grpc::MultiDenseVector>`, which reads `vectors[0].data.len()`. An empty `vectors` list panics:

```
index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0
```

at `lib/api/src/conversions/vectors.rs`. The other multi-dense conversions in the same file already use `MultiDenseVectorInternal::try_from_matrix`, which rejects an empty matrix.

## Fix

Route the `RawVector` `MultiDense` arm through `try_from_matrix` and return `invalid_argument`, matching the existing `Vector` conversion.

## Verification

`cargo test -p api --lib conversions::vectors::tests::empty_raw_multi_dense_vector_is_rejected -- --exact`

Before the change the test panicked with `index out of bounds: the len is 0 but the index is 0`. After the change it passes and the status is `InvalidArgument` with `MultiDenseVector cannot be empty`.

title: Bound cardinality estimates by the population they are adjusted to
body:
`adjust_to_available_vectors` and `adjust_for_deferred_points` cap `max` at the available points but only scale `exp`, so an incoming estimate above that population returns `exp > max`.

- Append-only deletion produces such estimates: a tombstone leaves the point's payload and field indexes in place, so the payload index still counts it while the id tracker does not (e.g. `exp: 30` for 22 available points)
- Debug builds trip the `exp <= max` assertion; release builds hand the inconsistent estimate to HNSW / ACORN and sparse search planning
- Fix: bound the estimate by the population before adjusting, after which the existing scaling keeps `min <= exp <= max`
- Found by the model tester with `--append-only-mutations` (#10773); regression test uses the numbers of that run and fails without the fix

title: Reject timeout=0 for write/update endpoints
body:
Fixes #9869

The OpenAPI schema declares timeout for write operations with minimum: 1, but the server accepted timeout=0 (zero) for all REST update endpoints. This aligns write endpoint behavior with read endpoints which already use NonZeroU64 for validation and reject zero timeout.

Changes:
- UpdateParams.timeout changed from Option<Duration> to Option<NonZeroU64> to automatically reject 0 during deserialization
- Added timeout() helper method returning Option<Duration>
- Added zero validation in gRPC from_grpc() conversion
- Updated all direct usages of params.timeout to use params.timeout()
- Fixed InferenceParams::new call sites in update_api handlers

title: Add upper-bound validation for shard_number, replication_factor, write_consistency_factor
body:
Fixes #9520

Creating a collection with shard_number=2147483647 (INT_MAX) causes the server to become unresponsive and crash while attempting to allocate resources for over 2 billion shards.

This change adds max=10000 validation to match the existing min=1 validation, returning a proper 422 validation error instead of crashing the server.

Changes:
- shard_number: add max=10000 range validation
- replication_factor: add max=10000 range validation  
- write_consistency_factor: add max=10000 range validation

## Summary
- Refactor payload-index schema transitions from `OnlyOnDiskFlipped` to `Compatible(CompatibleDiff)`, so `on_disk` and `enable_hnsw` flips (including combinations) share one shape instead of per-combination variants.

title: feat: tell a missing id tracker from an empty one
body:
## The problem

`detect_and_load` falls through to `ReadOnlyAppendableIdTracker::open` for a segment with no tracker
files, and that open tolerates their absence so a fresh segment loads. The result is an empty
tracker — total, available and deleted all zero — which is exactly what a segment that genuinely
holds nothing reports. A caller cannot tell "the tracker is not written yet" from "there is nothing
in here".

Outside `segment` the only workarounds are guessing from the point counts or hard-coding the tracker
file names, and which files make up a tracker is this module's business: it changes with the format.

Where it bites us: in the object-storage backend the optimizer reads each segment's tracker from the
bucket to decide what to optimize. A freshly created appendable segment is published to the manifest
before the first point is written into it, so it has objects but no tracker files — and it reads
back as an empty segment rather than one that cannot be assessed yet.

## The change

`is_persisted()` on `ReadOnlyIdTrackerEnum` and on `ReadOnlyAppendableIdTracker`. Purely additive,
no behaviour changes.

The appendable tracker answers from what a reload has actually read, not from whether it holds a
file handle. Over an object store the handle is handed out before the object is touched — a missing
log only reports itself from the first `len` or read, as `try_open`'s own doc notes — so the handles
cannot answer this. Both places that read a log's length set the flag, which makes the answer the
same on an eager backend and a lazy one.

The disk-resident and immutable variants only exist when their own `try_open` found the file that
defines the format, so they are always `true`.

A tracker emptied by deletes reports `true`: its logs are on disk, it just has no live points. That
is the case point counts cannot separate from the other two, which is why this is a separate
question and not a `total == 0` check.

## Tests

Three on the local filesystem (no storage, after a flush, emptied by deletes), and two over the
cached-blob stack — `DiskCacheFs` over `BlobFs` over an in-memory object store — which is where a
handle-based answer would be wrong: a segment with no objects at all must still report `false`.
`detect_and_load_selects_disk_format` now also asserts the flag for all three variants.

`cargo test -p segment --lib id_tracker`: 93 passed. `cargo clippy -p segment --all-targets`: clean.

title: [BM25] Query text indexes with a TextQuery through the Query API
body:
Makes BM25 over a scoring text index reachable from the Query API, REST and gRPC, with a canonical `TextQuery`. Part of #10750, stacked on #10785.

`POST /collections/books/points/query`

```json
{
  "query": { "text": "quick brown fox" },
  "using": "title",
  "limit": 10
}
```

```json
{
  "query": { "text": { "query": "quick brown fox", "k": 1.2, "b": 0.75 } },
  "using": "title",
  "limit": 10
}
```

- `TextQuery` message in proto (`Query.text = 12`, fields `query`, `k`, `b`); REST `TextInterface` is a string or the struct, normalized into one internal type, the `OrderByInterface` pattern. New parameters (`operator`, BM25F `fields`) land as fields of the message, never as a second spelling
- `using` is type-directed: a text query names a payload field, never a vector, so a vector and a field sharing a name do not interfere
- OR semantics: a point scores when it holds any query term; required or excluded terms go in `filter`
- Checked at the collection before any shard runs: `using` present, a text index with `scoring` on the field, `k >= 0` and `b` in `[0, 1]` (also schema-validated in REST and gRPC)
- Works at the root, in prefetches (hybrid RRF) and in query groups
- A `qdrant/bm25` document is unchanged and keeps the sparse route
- Scores use per-shard statistics (cross-shard IDF out of scope)
- OpenAPI regenerated
- Tests: openapi `test_bm25_text_index.py` (scores by definition, OR semantics, string and struct forms, filter, prefetch, groups, every refusal, vector name clash, bm25 document untouched), Rust unit tests for the checks and the normalization

title: Make the uio trace visualizer task-agnostic
body:
Stacked on #10769.

`tools/uio-trace-visualizer.html` no longer knows anything about segment layouts: every name, order and grouping comes from the trace file.

- **Lanes from the file tree.** Request paths form a tree, with single-child chains merged into one node. A side panel shows it with request counts and bytes per node. Clicking a node expands or collapses it; shift+click applies to its whole subtree; clicking a lane header does the same. A file with a `sections` event splits into one child per section. A directory's own requests (e.g. a `list` of a prefix whose files are also read) get their own lane, marked `·`. On load, the busiest nodes are expanded until there are about 12 lanes.
- **Ordering and colours from the trace.** Children follow the order of their first request in the file, and sections keep the layout's order. Colours are generated per tree node (golden-angle hues, three lightness levels), replacing the hard-coded `KIND_COLOR` table and the `classify()` path heuristics.
- **Filters.** A path filter takes a substring or a glob (`*` within a segment, `**` across segments; `/` focuses it), and there is one checkbox per operation found in the trace. The concurrency and bandwidth columns and the tree counts follow the filter.
- **Optional columns.** The phases and marks columns render only when the trace has phases or marks. The CPU column renders only when there are usable samples (on non-Linux they are all 0). Its bin is the median sampling interval taken from the trace, replacing the hard-coded 2 ms that went stale when the tracer moved to 10 ms in #10769.

## Testing

No real trace was available locally, so I generated two synthetic traces shaped like `edge-shard-query` output (two segments, a sectioned `links.bin`, a `list` and a `save`, with and without phases/marks/CPU) and drove the page in headless Chrome:
- Lanes, tree and columns are as expected for both traces.
- Tree click, shift+click and lane-header click expand and collapse correctly.
- The path glob and the op checkboxes filter correctly.
- The request tooltip and the sectioned file map render correctly.
- No page errors.

title: [BM25] Leave tombstoned points out of the text statistics
body:
Append-only deletion never reaches the text index, so `N`, `total_tokens` and `df` kept counting deleted points. Part of #10750.

- `fill_text_statistics` takes the id tracker's deleted bitslice and subtracts the deleted points the index still counts: from `N`, from the total (lengths read in one `doc_len_batch`), and from each query term's `df` (membership through one `check_match_batch` per term)
- `df` has to follow `N`: correcting `N` alone let `df` exceed it, clamping IDF to zero and scoring real matches at zero (found by the model tester's exact reference, #10773)
- Derived at gather time, no new mutation path: holds on the writer, after reload, and on read-only followers; deletions that reached the index are not subtracted twice
- The gather stops on cancellation during the scan
- Tests: gather over all three index shapes, and a segment test through `delete_point` with `append_only_mutations` on and off, checking `N`, `avgdl` and `df` (fails without the fix)

title: Report which algorithm ran a filtered graph search
body:
Add `filtered_acorn` to `VectorIndexSearchesTelemetry`.

title: Honor `exact` in Edge facet
body:
Follow-up to #10778, which found this while comparing each Edge read method with the server.

Edge `facet` ignored `exact`. It always added up the counts reported by each segment, and nothing at the segment level reads the flag. The server's local shard (`collection/src/shards/local_shard/facet.rs`) handles `exact: true` by collecting unique values across segments, then counting each value through `read_filtered` over all segments with the ids deduplicated. A point stored in several segments in different versions is then counted once.

Edge now does the same:
- It collects `unique_values` from every segment.
- It counts each value with the existing exact `count` (a `BTreeSet` of ids across segments) under `filter AND key == value`.
- It returns the top `limit` values via `FacetResponse::top_hits`.

### Test
`exact_facet_counts_filtered_values` checks the counts, `limit` and `filter` on the exact path. It doesn't fail on the old code: on a settled Edge shard the approximate and exact counts are the same. They only differ while a point is in two segments at once, during optimization, which is hard to set up in a unit test.

title: Fix Edge query offset and group hit payload/vectors
body:
Two places where Edge skipped post-processing that the server does at the collection level, above the shared shard code.

### `query()` ignored `offset`
`PlannedQuery` bumps the root limit to `limit + offset` and leaves cutting the offset to the caller (`collection/src/collection/query.rs`). Edge called the planner directly and never cut it, so `query(limit=1, offset=2)` returned the top 3 hits. `search()` was fine because its edge path already drains the offset.

The offset is now dropped in `resolve_plan`, before payload/vectors are filled, so skipped points aren't fetched. This covers `query` and `query_batch`. Grouping and the matrix API always use `offset: 0`.

The existing batch test with `.offset(2)` didn't catch this because it only compares batched and one-by-one results, which were both wrong in the same way.

### `query_groups()` ignored `with_payload` / `with_vector`
The group-by driver fetches candidates with only the `group_by` field as payload. The server hydrates the final hits with the requested payload and vectors after `distill()` (`collection/src/grouping/group_by.rs`). Edge returned the candidates as they were. Edge now does the same as the server: candidates are fetched without vectors, and the distinct final hits are filled once.

### Checked, no change needed
scroll (point-id offset, handled), search, count, retrieve, search_matrix.

### Not fixed here
`facet` ignores `exact` on Edge: it always merges per-segment approximate counts. The server does exact per-value counts through `read_filtered` in that case.

### Tests
- `query_skips_offset`: fails without the fix (`[4, 3, 2]` vs `[2]`)
- `group_hits_carry_requested_payload_and_vectors`: fails without the fix (missing `extra` payload key)

title: Cap ACORN's 2-hop bridges per candidate at m0, like its 1-hop matches
body:
`search_on_level_acorn` splits a candidate's neighbours in two: those that pass the
filter are scored, **capped at `hop1_limit` (= `m0`)**, and those that fail it are
walked through into their own neighbours — **uncapped**.

```rust
if points_scorer.filters().check_vector(hop1) {
    to_score.push(hop1);
    if to_score.len() >= hop1_limit {
        return ControlFlow::Break(());       // matches: capped
    }
} else {
    to_explore.push(hop1);                   // bridges: unbounded
}
```

The `Break` only fires when the *matching* half fills up, so under a selective
filter it never fires and the loop walks the entire adjacency list, turning every
non-matching neighbour into a 2-hop expansion.

That is fine on a plain graph, where a point has at most `m0` links. It is not fine
on a collection built with `payload_m`: `merge_from_other` appends each payload
block's links to the same level-0 list **without re-pruning**, so a point can carry
several hundred links, and one candidate becomes hundreds of adjacency reads plus
the filter checks and scoring behind them.

This PR applies `hop1_limit` to both halves of the split.

## Why the first `m0` links are the right ones to keep

The links a point starts with are the ones the build's pruning heuristic selected;
the per-payload-value links are appended after them. Truncating therefore keeps the
neighbours the graph actually chose, and drops the tail that was concatenated on.

On a collection without payload links the whole list is at most `m0`, so the cap
can never bind — **this is a no-op there by construction**.

## Benchmark

Three binaries built with `--release`: this PR's patch, its merge base `1f0b3de`, and this PR's first version, which lacked the unvisit (used to isolate the visited-list change). All three served bit-identical copies of each collection side by side on one CCX43, and every query went to all three in rotating order.

**Null control.** Plain filtered HNSW ran alongside, since this PR does not touch that path:
- identical results in 70,200 of 70,200 cross-binary comparisons
- recall change of exactly 0
- speed ratio: median ×1.01

**Setup.**
- 1M points per dataset, `payload_m` default, `m` ∈ {8, 16, 32}
- nine filters from 50% down to 1%, including two-field conjunctions
- `ef` swept from 16 to 512; 200 queries per filter (arXiv: 60 per selectivity band)
- Speedup is p50 at the cheapest `ef` reaching recall 0.95, with a paired-bootstrap 95% interval.

**Summary: `acorn` row, speedup at matched recall 0.95, median across the filter conditions**

- **arXiv 5–20% (×0.78) and deep 1% AND are step artifacts** of "cheapest `ef` reaching 0.95": one binary lands just under the target and needs the next `ef`, which is why both intervals are wide.
- **<0.1%:** the planner runs an exact scan, so the graph is not touched.
- **The unvisit is free:** against this PR's first version, the recall ceiling agrees within 0.005 in all 69 cells and speed agrees at a median ×1.01.
- **Random vectors lose some recall ceiling**, up to −0.086 (in 6 of 24 cells by ≥0.02). With no cluster structure, the surplus links there were genuine routes. Real-vector datasets show at most −0.002.
- **At equal `ef`** the cap is about 2× cheaper, but at low `ef` it finds fewer neighbours. Matched recall is the fair comparison, and it is the one reported above.
- **Absolute latencies are 2–3× higher than in isolated runs:** streams ran concurrently, and each binary was pinned to one physical core shared with the other two. The claim is the ratio.

Raw per-query CSVs, receipts and the harness: https://github.com/qdrant/end-to-end-large-benches/tree/results/acorn-score-gate/results/acorn-score-gate (pass four, `raw_ab/`).

## Visited-list semantics

One rule for both caps: **a link a cap skips stays unvisited**, whether it is a match past the `m0`-th or a bridge past the `m0`-th. A cap changes what one candidate expands, never what the search can reach, so a skipped link can still be taken from another candidate.

- **In-memory path:** a link is marked visited only when it is admitted for scoring or expansion. For matches this was already true, since the loop `Break`s before touching the rest of the list.
- **Batched path:** the whole batch is marked during the batched collection, before the split, so links over quota are unvisited. That is what `admit_matches` already does for matches.

**Measured:** against marking skipped bridges visited, the recall ceiling agrees within 0.005 in all 69 cells and speed agrees at a median ×1.01. The rule is chosen for its semantics; performance does not distinguish the two.

**Why the cap keeps the right links.** `merge_from_other` appends payload-block links after the base graph's own. Compressed storage sorts the first `m0` links for delta encoding, but keeps them in front. So the bridges kept are the base graph's own non-matching neighbours, and the ones dropped are other fields' payload-block links. Those are pruned only within their block and mostly fail the filter.

**Separate, pre-existing:** under a filter, the two paths can pick different bridges. The in-memory loop stops collecting bridges at the `m0`-th match, while the batched path collects them from the whole list. That was already true before this PR; I can file it separately.

## Context

This came out of an investigation into whether ideas from the PathSeer PR (#10701)
could be lifted into ACORN one at a time. A second idea from that work — scoring a
filtered-out neighbour and skipping it when it scores below the result set — is
worth a further ×2 on top of this on 96-dimensional collections, but it reverses
sign by 1536 dimensions, so it is not proposed here. This PR is only the part that
is unconditionally safe.

title: test(segment): pin graph_inline_storage HNSW build to 1 CPU and seed 42
body:
## Problem

`test_graph_inline_storage_contract::case_3_u8` (Uint8 + Mmap) is flaky in CI. The assertion at line 277 (`common + 2 >= TOP`, TOP=10) needs 8 of the 10 exact nearest neighbors in the approximate result. The reported failure on 2026-09-24 had only 6 in common:

```
[103, 132, 161, 288, 347, 366, 473, 543, 565, 595] vs [132, 153, 161, 173, 366, 432, 473, 543, 565, 595]
```

## Root cause

The input vectors are already seeded (`StdRng::seed_from_u64(4242)`), but the HNSW graph built for the indexed segment is not deterministic. `build_indexed` calls `SegmentBuilder::build_for_test`, which does two things:

- It passes `ResourcePermit::dummy(get_num_indexing_threads(0))`, so the permit covers every CPU on the machine. The graph build pool is sized from `permit.num_cpus` (`lib/segment/src/index/hnsw_index/hnsw/build.rs:146`), not from `max_indexing_threads` in the test config. Setting that field to 1 does not make the build single-threaded.
- It uses an unseeded `rand::rng()`, and point levels are drawn from that RNG (`build.rs:161`).

So the graph changes from run to run and from runner to runner. For the Uint8 case the recall margin is small enough that some graphs miss the threshold.

My first version of this PR pinned `max_indexing_threads` to 1. That was wrong for the reason above, and it is reverted here.

## Fix

`build_indexed` now calls `SegmentBuilder::build` directly with `ResourcePermit::dummy(1)` and `StdRng::seed_from_u64(42)`. With one CPU and a fixed seed, the graph is the same on every run. `max_indexing_threads` is back to 2, as on `dev`.

## Testing

- `cargo test -p segment --test integration graph_inline_storage_test::test_graph_inline_storage_contract`: all 6 cases pass.
- I ran `case_3_u8` 20 times with the fix on a GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest` runner: 20 passed, 0 failed.
- For reference, the unfixed test also passed 20/20 on the same runner, so the flake did not show up on that machine. The fix removes both sources of variation rather than relying on the failure rate being low.
- `cargo +nightly fmt --all --check`: clean.

## Scope

Test-only change. No production code touched.

Fixes #10774

title: [Feature Request]: Nano (XNO) payment for Qdrant Cloud Inference API
body:
## Describe the problem

Qdrant Cloud's Inference API uses paid models for embeddings (remote inference with `cloud_inference=True`). Users are billed for inference tokens — a metered, per-token API that AI agents call at high frequency. For autonomous agents that need per-operation payment authority, paying for each inference request in USD or USDC means per-transaction fees that make micropayments uneconomical.

The Qdrant Python client (`qdrant-client`) already supports inference via `Document` models — `client.upsert(collection_name, points=[PointStruct(id=1, payload={\"topic\": \"cooking\"}, vector=Document(text=\"...\", model=\"<model>\"))])`. Each such call triggers a paid inference. Agents that embed at scale accumulate many such micropayments.

## Describe the proposed solution

Add **Nano (XNO) payment support** for Qdrant Cloud's Inference API, integrated through the client library.

Concretely:

1. **A Nano-payment-aware client option** that intercepts inference calls (when `cloud_inference=True` and a model is specified), derives a per-request Nano payment via x402 (using the existing feeless402 library — `github.com/michardnicolas/feeless402`), and submits the payment before the inference call. Drop-in: `client = QdrantClient(url=..., api_key=..., cloud_inference=True, payment='nano')` instead of the current constructor.

2. **For Qdrant**: accept Nano as a billing currency for inference tokens. Agents that already hold XNO can pay for inference without converting to USD, avoiding fee erosion that makes sub-cent micropayments uneconomical.

## Alternatives considered

- **USDC on Base via x402**: gas fees exceed micropayment value.
- **Credit card billing**: aggregated monthly — not per-operation.
- **Do nothing**: agents infer until the bill comes due.

## Importance

- **would make my life easier** — high-frequency embedding workloads where each inference should be paid for in real time by the agent itself.

## Additional context

- `feeless402` (MIT) provides fee-free x402 micropayments in Nano — `github.com/michardnicolas/feeless402`.
- Nano: fee-free, <1s settlement, self-custodied.
- A working Nano x402 adapter for the OpenAI Agents SDK exists — `github.com/dhyabi2/openai-agents-nano-x402`.

title: fix: return non-positive distance in binary quantization for L1 and L2
body:
Binary quantization previously returned cosine similarity (`zeros_count - xor_product`) for L1 and L2 metrics, producing positive values for close vectors. When `rescore=false`, Euclidean post-processing (`abs().sqrt()`) folded positive scores, causing exact matches to report larger distances than partial matches and violating score monotonicity. Returning `-xor_product` adheres to the metric contract that similarity is non-positive distance, preserving HNSW traversal ordering while ensuring post-processed Euclidean scores remain monotonic.

Fixes #10607

title: [BM25] Query BM25 over the text index in the model tester
body:
Stacked on #10770. A `QueryText` op for the model tester (#10750): BM25 over `t` through `ScoringQuery::Text`, the path a text query takes through the planner, the shards and the per-source merge, checked against the model's scores.

- the eager `t` index sets `scoring`; per seed, its placement once optimized (`Memory::Pinned` / `Memory::Cold`) and one of six tokenizer variants: default `Word`, case-sensitive `Whitespace`, English stopwords + Snowball stemmer + ASCII folding, token length limits, `Prefix`, `Multilingual`
- `t` documents repeat terms and vary in length (1 to 12 words), sometimes as arrays, empty, or capitalized, from a vocabulary those variants change (stems, stopwords, an accent, short and long words, punctuation); the model tokenizes with the field's own tokenizer and checks everything after it
- queries are 1 to 3 words, `k1` and `b` drawn down to zero half the time, optional `num` / `url` prefix filters
- across the collection: every result is live, passes the filter and holds a query term; no id repeats; ranked best first; complete when the matches fit below `SHARD_QUERY_SUBSAMPLING_LIMIT` (made `pub(crate)`)
- per shard, whatever the statistics: equal term frequencies and length score the same; a dominating document never scores lower; every score fits one IDF per term and one average length, recovered from the points holding a single query term
- across queries, when a shard's ranking is the same before and after: the top 1, top k and top 10 match the full ranking, and the collection's top matches the shards' merge
- exact BM25 by definition over the model's documents whenever a shard's statistics are exact: no proxy (optimizer off and no snapshot in flight, or a segment layout with none, unchanged around the queries) and no deleted point left in an immutable segment's postings
- the soak binary and the harness default to an indexing threshold of 1 KB: at 5 KB no vector crossed it inside a 10 KB segment, so no segment became non-appendable and the immutable and on-disk text indexes never served a query
- `--append-only-mutations` turns on tombstone-only deletion for the soak binary

Mutation-tested with `--swarm-interval 250` (a run otherwise draws one op subset, and about half never enable `QueryText`): on-disk lengths read at the wrong offset caught 3/3, mutable lengths +1 2/2, a too-tight MaxScore bound 2/2; no false positives on 8 clean seeds across all tokenizer variants and placements. Soaks found a real bug, `df` counting append-only tombstones after `N` stopped (fixed in #10782), and an estimator bug outside BM25 (#10794). The CI harness gates pass, `harness_no_restarts` in the same time as before.

title: Meter remote requests and expose IO statistics to edge shard users
body:
Follow-up to #10637. That PR counted the disk cache's logical fetches. This one replaces that with a single layer that counts every remote request issued through `BlobFs` and `BlobFile`, writes included, so an application using `ReadOnlyEdgeShard` or `UpdateOnlyEdgeShard` can read cumulative IO totals.

### Design

- `common::universal_io::OpStats` holds lock-free atomic counters for one operation kind: started, completed, not_found, errors, abandoned, bytes, and a latency histogram. An RAII `OpGuard` counts an operation dropped before finishing as abandoned. Snapshots are plain loads, with no background thread.
  - `not_found` is separate from `errors`, because "does not exist" is the expected answer to existence and length probes of new objects.
- `io_bridge::RemoteIoStats` has one `OpStats` per `uio_trace::Op`. `Op` gains `create`, `remove`, `save` and `append`, and derives strum's `EnumCount`/`EnumIter`/`IntoStaticStr` in place of a hand-maintained `ALL` array.
  - A `RequestObserver` at each remote call site drives the trace request and the stats guard together, so the trace visualizer also shows writes. It classifies errors through `IsNotFound`, and the trace records a matching `not_found` outcome.
  - One `append` or `save` counts as one request however the backend performs it. Backend retries and part-copy fallbacks are left for a later layer.
- `DiskCacheStats` is removed. Every disk-cache fetch is exactly one `BlobFile` read that `RemoteIoStats` already counts, so the cache counters duplicated the remote `read`/`read_from` counters.
  - `CachedBlobFs::stats()` returns `RemoteIoStats` directly. Both halves of the filesystem share one observer, which is why `from_context` now opens the backend once and delegates to `new`.
  - `DiskCacheFs::remote_fs()` gives callers that hold a plain disk cache access to the remote half.
  - `ReadOnlyEdgeShard::fs()` and `UpdateOnlyEdgeShard::fs()` expose the filesystem.
- `read_from` of a tail at or past EOF (every whole read of an empty object) records its outcome only after the `len` probe. It counts as a completed empty read rather than an error. A NotFound failure skips the probe, since a missing object cannot have an empty tail.
- `CachedBlobFile`'s whole-object rewrite moved onto `BlobFile::save_whole`, which resolves the TODO there and puts the rewrite path under metering.
- The uio-trace writer samples process CPU every 10 ms instead of every 2 ms.

### Tools

- `edge-shard-update` logs the IO counters moved by open, schema read, preview or apply, followed by the totals, on the object-storage backends.
- `edge-shard-query` prints the per-phase remote request counters, with a latency histogram per operation.
- Both tools set the global feature flags to `serverless_compatible` at startup. Previously they ran with the flags uninitialized, which logged "Feature flags not initialized" and fell back to defaults.

### Validation

- [x] Targets `dev`; rebased onto the current `dev` tip.
- [x] `cargo test -p io_bridge -p io_bridge_object_store`: 37 + 51 passed. This includes per-op counting with `not_found`, a NotFound `read_from` issuing no `len` probe, and an empty-object whole read counting as completed against the in-memory object store.
- [x] `cargo test -p common --lib -- universal_io op_stats uio_trace`.
- [x] `cargo clippy` on the touched crates with `--all-targets --all-features -D warnings`.
- [x] `cargo +nightly fmt --all -- --check`.

Not done yet: metering at the backend HTTP layer inside `io_bridge_object_store` (retries, part-copy fan-out, wire bytes). Prometheus exposition is deliberately out of scope for now.

title: [BM25] Merge BM25 over a text index across shards
body:
Stacked on #10765. Phase 4c of #10750: `ScoringQuery::Text` carries a BM25 query through the universal query path, per local shard, to remote shards, and merged across shards by the existing per-source k-merge. No public API sends one yet (query interface is separate).

- planner: `PlannedQuery::texts` and `Source::TextsIdx`, a bare leaf like a search, at the root or as a prefetch, so it fuses with dense prefetches (hybrid search)
- `MergePlan::validate` refuses Text as a rescore at any level: scoring a set of prefetched points by BM25 has no path yet
- local shard: text leaves run concurrently with searches and scrolls, cut at the leaf's score threshold (strict `>`), priced like a scroll by the read rate limiter
- internal gRPC: `TextScoringInternal { field, text, k1, b }` in the `QueryShardPoints` oneof, converted both ways; the raw text travels so each shard tokenizes with its own schema
- edge refuses it for now; its FFI and Python exhaustiveness guards mark the variant as not exposed
- tests: planner leaves and refusals, the gRPC round trip, and through a collection: one shard against BM25 by definition, two shards against each shard merged, pagination, and RRF with a dense prefetch
- a corpus-scoped `idf` on a text query is refused, at the root and as a prefetch, instead of being dropped silently: text statistics cover the whole collection, which is what the default `idf` scope means

The collection-level scores are checked with `b` inert, since nothing records lengths until the `scoring` index param lands. Rolling upgrades: an old node answers "missing field: score" to a Text query, harmless while nothing can send one.
